definition.text: A sampling distribution is the probability distribution of a statistic obtained from many samples drawn from a population.

anchor.quote: the probability distribution of a statistic obtained from a large number of samples drawn from a specific population

facts.text: The central limit theorem states the sampling distribution of the mean approaches normal as sample size increases, regardless of population shape.

anchor.quote: the sampling distribution of the sample mean approaches a normal distribution as the sample size increases, regardless of the shape of the population distribution

facts.text: The standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the mean equals the population standard deviation divided by the square root of the sample size.

anchor.quote: the population standard deviation divided by the square root of the sample size

misconceptions.text: Students believe a larger sample makes the population itself normal, rather than the sampling distribution of the mean.

examples.text: Averaging 40 dice rolls many times yields a near-normal distribution of averages even though a single roll is uniform.

mcBank.stem: According to the central limit theorem, increasing the sample size makes the sampling distribution of the mean
options: closer to normal and narrower
closer to the population shape
wider and more skewed
identical to a single observation

mapping.population: the full population the samples are drawn from
mapping.sample: each sample drawn from the population
mapping.statistic: the sample mean across repeated samples
mapping.uncertainty: the sampling variability captured by the standard deviation of the sampling distribution

definition.text: A p-value is the probability of obtaining a test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed, assuming the null hypothesis is true.

anchor.quote: the probability of obtaining a test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed, assuming the null hypothesis is true

facts.text: A small p-value indicates the observed data would be unlikely under the null hypothesis.

anchor.quote: A small p-value indicates that the observed data would be unlikely under the null hypothesis

facts.text: The p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true, and it does not measure effect size.

anchor.quote: The p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true, and it does not measure the size of an effect

misconceptions.text: Students interpret the p-value as the probability that the null hypothesis is true.
misconceptions.corrective: It is a probability about the data given the null, not about the hypothesis given the data.

examples.text: A p-value of 0.03 means data this extreme would occur 3 percent of the time if the null were true.

mcBank.stem: A study reports p = 0.02. Which interpretation is correct?
options: Data this extreme would be unlikely if the null hypothesis were true
There is a 2 percent chance the null hypothesis is true
The effect is large
The result will replicate 98 percent of the time

mapping.population: the population under the null hypothesis
mapping.statistic: the test statistic computed from the observed data
mapping.uncertainty: the probability of data at least as extreme assuming the null hypothesis is true

definition.text: A statistical model is a simplified mathematical representation of how data are generated.

anchor.quote: a simplified mathematical representation of how data are generated

facts.text: A model such as linear regression keeps a few structural features and discards others, relying on assumptions like linearity and independent errors.

anchor.quote: keeps a few structural features and discards others, relying on assumptions like linearity and independent errors

facts.text: When those assumptions fail, the model's conclusions can be misleading even if it fits the sample well.

anchor.quote: the model's conclusions can be misleading even if it fits the sample well

misconceptions.text: Students trust a model that fits the sample well, overlooking that broken assumptions can still make its conclusions wrong.
misconceptions.corrective: Good fit does not guarantee valid assumptions; check the assumptions, not just the fit.

examples.text: A regression with strong R-squared can still mislead if the errors are not independent.

mcBank.stem: A statistical model can mislead even with good fit when
options: its key assumptions fail
the sample is very large
it is written in math
it reports an R-squared

mapping.model: a statistical model such as linear regression
mapping.kept features: a few structural features of how the data are generated
mapping.discarded features: the other influences the model omits
mapping.breaking assumption: assumptions like linearity and independent errors

definition.text: An observational study measures variables without assigning treatments, so an association it finds may be due to a confounding variable rather than a causal effect.

anchor.quote: an association it finds may be due to a confounding variable rather than a causal effect

facts.text: A confounding variable influences both the supposed cause and the supposed effect, creating a spurious association.

anchor.quote: influences both the supposed cause and the supposed effect, creating a spurious association

facts.text: Establishing causation generally requires ruling out confounders, often through a randomized experiment.

anchor.quote: Establishing causation generally requires ruling out confounders, often through a randomized experiment

misconceptions.text: Students read a strong association in an observational study as proof of cause, without considering a confounder.
misconceptions.corrective: Association is not causation until plausible confounders are ruled out.

examples.text: Ice-cream sales and drowning rise together, but the confounder is summer heat, not a causal link.

mcBank.stem: A strong association in an observational study is not proof of causation because
options: a confounding variable may explain it
the sample was too small
associations are always false
the data were written down

mapping.association: an association measured in the observational study
mapping.proposed cause: the variable treated as the cause
mapping.proposed effect: the variable treated as the effect

definition.text: Data provenance is the record of where a dataset came from: who collected it, by what method, and for what purpose.

anchor.quote: Data provenance is the record of where a dataset came from: who collected it, by what method, and for what purpose

facts.text: The collection method and its purpose can bias what the data can support.

anchor.quote: the collection method and its purpose can bias what the data can support

facts.text: Conclusions are only as trustworthy as the provenance of the data behind them.

anchor.quote: Conclusions are only as trustworthy as the provenance of the data behind them

misconceptions.text: Students treat a dataset as objective fact, ignoring how the collection method and purpose shape what it can support.
misconceptions.corrective: Ask who collected the data, how, and why before trusting what the numbers say.

examples.text: A customer-satisfaction survey emailed only to repeat buyers overstates satisfaction, because its provenance excludes the unhappy customers who already left.

mcBank.stem: Before trusting the numbers in a dataset, a statistician first asks
options: who collected it, how, and for what purpose
whether the spreadsheet file opens without any errors
whether the reported numbers are large
whether the average is a round value

mapping.maker and context: who collected the data and how
mapping.intended audience: the purpose the data were collected for
mapping.what it can support: the conclusions the data can credibly support

definition.text: A confidence interval is an interval estimate for an unknown population parameter.

anchor.quote: an interval estimate for an unknown population parameter

facts.text: The confidence level is the percent expression for the probability that the interval contains the true population parameter.

anchor.quote: the percent expression for the probability that the confidence interval contains the true population parameter

facts.text: The margin of error depends on the confidence level, the sample size, and the population standard deviation.

anchor.quote: depends on the confidence level, sample size, and known or estimated population standard deviation

facts.text: A point estimate is a single number computed from a sample and used to estimate a population parameter.

anchor.quote: a single number computed from a sample and used to estimate a population parameter

facts.text: A confidence interval depends on the desired confidence level, what is known about the distribution, and the sample size.

anchor.quote: the desired confidence level, information that is known about the distribution

misconceptions.text: Students read a 95% confidence interval as a 95% probability that the parameter lies inside the one interval they computed.
misconceptions.corrective: The confidence level describes the procedure across repeated samples — at CL = 90%, in 90 out of 100 samples the interval estimate encloses the parameter — rather than a probability attached to a single interval already calculated.

examples.text: A poll reporting 46% support with a three-point margin of error at 95% confidence describes how often intervals built this way capture the true share, not the odds for this one poll.

mcBank.stem: A 95% confidence level tells you that
options: intervals built this way capture the parameter 95% of the time
this particular interval has a 95% chance of being right now
95% of the sampled observations fall inside the interval
the sample mean equals the population mean in 95% of cases

attribution: OpenStax, Introductory Statistics 2e, Ch. 8 Key Terms

definition.text: A histogram is a graphical representation in x-y form of the distribution of data in a data set.

anchor.quote: a graphical representation in x-y form of the distribution of data in a data set

facts.text: In a histogram the x-axis carries the data and the y-axis the frequency, and the graph consists of contiguous rectangles.

anchor.quote: x represents the data and y represents the frequency, or relative frequency. The graph consists of contiguous rectangles

facts.text: A box plot gives a quick picture of the middle 50% of the data.

anchor.quote: a graph that gives a quick picture of the middle 50% of the data

facts.text: An outlier is an observation that does not fit the rest of the data.

anchor.quote: an observation that does not fit the rest of the data

facts.text: Relative frequency is the ratio of the times a value occurs to the number of all outcomes.

anchor.quote: the ratio of the number of times a value of the data occurs in the set of all outcomes to the number of all outcomes

misconceptions.text: Students read a histogram like a bar chart of separate categories and treat the spacing between bars as meaningless decoration.
misconceptions.corrective: A histogram's rectangles are contiguous because the horizontal axis carries continuous data, so a visible gap reports an interval with zero frequency rather than a break between unrelated categories.

examples.text: A histogram of commute times shows the shape of the whole distribution, while a box plot of the same data shows where the middle half sits and flags observations that do not fit the rest.

mcBank.stem: Histogram rectangles are drawn contiguously because
options: the horizontal axis represents a continuous data range
every interval is required to contain at least one observation
the vertical axis always shows relative frequency
adjacent categories are unrelated to one another

attribution: OpenStax, Introductory Statistics 2e, Ch. 2 Key Terms
